"Concurrent" means happening, existing, or taking place at the same time. When two or more things are concurrent, they overlap in time — they run alongside each other rather than one coming after the other.

Think of it this way: if two movies are playing in two different theaters in the same building right now, those are concurrent showings. Neither one waits for the other to finish. They coexist in the same window of time.
The key idea: alongside, not after

The most important thing to understand about "concurrent" is what it stands against — and that's the idea of things being consecutive (one after the other). Concurrent things are like lanes on a highway, running side by side at the same time. Consecutive things are like cars in a single lane, following each other in a line.

Here are a few clear everyday examples. "The company ran two concurrent investigations" means both investigations were active at the same time — not one finished before the other began. "She was juggling three concurrent projects at work" means all three were ongoing simultaneously. "The two storms were concurrent, making the system especially dangerous" means both storms existed at the same time and overlapped.
Concurrent in law

One of the most common places you will encounter this word is in legal contexts, especially criminal sentencing. When a judge orders concurrent sentences, the prison terms for multiple crimes are served at the same time, overlapping each other.

For example: if someone is convicted of two crimes and receives a 10-year sentence for the first and a 5-year sentence for the second, and the judge orders them to run concurrently, the person serves only 10 years total. The shorter sentence is absorbed into the longer one because both run at the same time. If the judge had ordered them to run consecutively instead, the person would serve 10 + 5 = 15 years, back to back. This distinction matters enormously in courtrooms.

"Concurrent jurisdiction" is another legal use — it describes a situation where two courts (say, a federal court and a state court) both have the legal authority to hear the same case at the same time, without one excluding the other.
Concurrent in computing and technology

In computer science, "concurrent" is a major technical concept. It refers to multiple processes or tasks being handled at the same time, or in overlapping time periods, by a system. When your phone plays music while downloading an app, displaying notifications, and syncing your email all at once — that is concurrency at work.

"Concurrent programming" is actually a significant and challenging field of computer science, precisely because coordinating multiple things happening at once without them colliding or interfering with each other is genuinely complex. You may see phrases like "concurrent processes," "concurrent threads," or "concurrent execution" in technical writing.
Concurrent in geometry

In geometry, "concurrent" has a precise technical meaning that is slightly different from the general one. Three or more lines are called concurrent when they all pass through a single common point. Note that here, the word is not about time at all — it is about lines meeting at one shared location. For example, the three angle bisectors of any triangle always meet at a single point, so they are described as concurrent lines. This is a domain-specific use of the word that geometry textbooks use often.
The less common meaning: agreement or acting together

"Concurrent" can also describe things that agree with each other or work in conjunction. This meaning is rarer in everyday speech but you may see it in formal or official writing. For instance, "a concurrent resolution" in a legislature is one passed by both chambers (like a Senate and a House of Representatives) together, with both acting at the same time toward the same goal.
What "concurrent" does NOT mean

It does not mean identical. Two things can happen at the same time while being completely different from each other. It does not mean related or connected — two events can be concurrent purely by coincidence, with no link between them. And most importantly, it does not mean consecutive or sequential. That is its direct opposite.
How it compares to similar words

Simultaneous is the closest synonym, but it usually implies things happening at the very same instant. "Concurrent" is broader — it can describe things that overlap across a stretch of time. Two explosions happening at 3:00:00 PM are simultaneous. Two construction projects running across the same six months are concurrent.

Parallel is also close in meaning and suggests things running alongside each other, often independently. It is slightly more structural or visual in feel. "Parallel investigations" and "concurrent investigations" mean nearly the same thing, but "parallel" hints more at independence.

Contemporaneous means existing in the same time period, and is used more in historical or academic writing. ("The two empires were contemporaneous.") It is broader and less about active overlap.

Coexisting simply means existing at the same time, without implying any particular interaction or relationship.
The antonyms
The clear opposites of concurrent are consecutive, sequential, successive, and serial — all of which describe things happening one after the other, in an ordered line, rather than at the same time.
The word family

Concurrently (adverb) — "The two trials proceeded concurrently." This is how you describe the action or state.

Concurrence (noun) — The state of things happening at the same time, or agreement between people or parties. "The concurrence of two major events on the same day created chaos."

Concur (verb) — To happen at the same time, or to agree with someone. "I concur with your assessment" is a formal way of saying "I agree." "The two events concurred" means they happened at the same time.
A quick summary to lock it in

Concurrent = at the same time, overlapping, running in parallel. Its opposite is consecutive = one after another, in sequence. You will find it in everyday speech, law, technology, and geometry, and while the flavor shifts slightly across these fields, the heart of the word stays the same: multiple things sharing the same window of time.
